pieces.title: Thirty years on the road, he turned landscape into a record that can be checked: Xu Xiake
pieces.hook: Turn “I have been there” into “this is what I saw”: the value of travel is not how far you go, but whether the record can be checked…
pieces.takeaway: Turn “I have been there” into “this is what I saw”: the value of travel is not how far you go, but whether later readers can check the record.
pieces.imageCredit: Anonymous (historical portrait, reproduced by User:Mountain) · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Xu Xiake (given name Hongzu, courtesy name Zhenzhi, 1587–1641) was a traveler and geographer of the Ming dynasty, from Jiangyin in Jiangsu. He did not spend his life on the civil-service exams or official office. Instead he spent about thirty years walking, observing, and keeping a diary. The Xu Xiake’s Travels that later readers see is not a lyrical landscape sketch. It is much closer to a field record that can be checked.

paras.lead: His mother agreed to the journeys
parts: He was born in 1587 into a scholarly family in Jiangyin. After failing the exams several times as a young man, he turned to travel. The family did not simply look the other way: his mother, Lady Wang, supported the trips and agreed on dates for his return.

That support mattered. In a society that treated official office as the proper path, thirty years of travel required the family’s financial and moral tolerance. His routes ran from near to far, from the Jiangnan region and North China to the more distant southwest, covering what are now more than ten provinces and regions.

The last journey, and the most important one: in 1636, when he was about fifty, he set out again, focusing on what are now Guangxi, Guizhou, and Yunnan, until he was sent home ill around 1640. That southwestern journey let him observe karst (limestone) landscapes systematically.

He recorded more than two hundred caves, and noted that many caverns were formed by flowing water, and that stalactites were the result of calcium-bearing droplets slowly building up. Those judgments came earlier than later systematic karst research in Europe, which is why modern earth scientists regard him as one of the field’s pioneers.

Along the way he recorded the run of mountain ranges, the sources of rivers, rocks, vegetation, and routes, and he corrected some older claims that had rested only on hearsay. His observations of water systems such as the upper Yangtze and the North and South Pan Rivers were later often cited as examples of “checking with one’s own eyes.” The diary also mentions hunger, thirst, bandits, and illness, which shows that these pages were not imagined in a study.

The writing is in diary form. Friends later edited it; about 600,000 characters survive, and some chapters were lost in transmission. He died at home in 1641, at the age of 54. Only long after his death did the travel record gradually receive attention. After scholars in the Qing period and in modern times edited it, this private diary entered a wider academic view.
He left no official post, but he left a method: to judge geography, go and look at the place itself, and write down what you see, so later people can test it.

items: Set out to survey the southwest
Died; later editors turned the diary into a book

blocks.title: A few years from Xu Xiake’s travels
items: Set out to survey the southwest

critical.label: Another angle
items: Xu Xiake｜View: Landscapes have to be seen in person, not taken only from books and legends.；Stakes: Turn observations into a complete record.；Worry: Illness, bandits, and a journey cut short.；Basis: A long-running diary; on-the-spot analysis of caves and rivers.

The family, especially his mother｜View: He may go, but the family must still have an ethical account of it.；Stakes: The son’s safety and his dates of return.；Worry: A long journey with no return, and no one to look after the household.；Basis: His mother’s support and limits on his travel while she lived.

The examination and official-career society｜View: The proper path for a scholar is official office.；Stakes: Keep the existing standard of success.；Worry: Talent is “wasted” on wandering.；Basis: After failing the exams several times he changed course, and never followed the usual official path.

Later geographers｜View: These diaries are early scientific observations.；Stakes: A thread for the history of earth science in China.；Worry: Treating a literary travel record as if it were fully scientific, or ignoring missing text.；Basis: Modern earth science’s reappraisal of his karst notes.

Readers and local commemoration｜View: He is a symbol of travel, and a cultural resource for his hometown.；Stakes: Tourism, remembrance, and identity.；Worry: Remembering only that he “walked the famous mountains,” and forgetting that he was writing about geology and hydrology.；Basis: The wide publication of the travels, and the founding of related memorial sites.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: Family support made the journeys possible; family concern also framed when he left and when he came back.
The more specific the diary, the more scientific value it has—and the easier it is to lose or alter in editing and copying.
He corrected older claims by walking a certain range; however large that range, it was still only what one person in one era could reach.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: “Seeing in person” is powerful, but it cannot cover places he never reached. For the science to continue, one person’s diary has to become measurements that others can repeat.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Exact counts of the provinces and regions he covered are not fully consistent, because administrative boundaries have changed and some chapters are missing.
Some of the diary was already incomplete in the early Qing; the text we have today has been edited.
Calling him “the first person in the world to study karst” would need a stricter comparison of international scholarly history. This article uses only “one of the pioneers.”

pieces.title: How a map flattens the world: two thousand years of cartography
pieces.hook: Before you use a map, ask for whom it was flattened: a projection that helps navigation can also give people a false idea of the world’s shape.
pieces.takeaway: Before you use a map, ask for whom it was flattened: a projection that helps navigation can also give people a false idea of the world’s shape.
pieces.imageCredit: Gerardus Mercator · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The earth is round; paper is flat. Any world map has to give something up: area is distorted, or direction is distorted, or both are compromised. A map looks like just a picture. It is actually a product of surveying, mathematics, power, and printing.
Who draws it, what is drawn, and what is left out often depend on who will use the map.

paras.lead: China wrote cartography into rules early on
parts: Pei Xiu of the Western Jin set out the “Six Principles of Cartography,” discussing scale, orientation, distance, and related rules. That is often seen as an important starting point for traditional Chinese map theory. Later dynasties produced national or regional maps, with accuracy limited by surveying tools and projection methods. In the Kangxi reign of the Qing, the court organized nationwide field surveys from 1708 to 1718 and completed the Huangyu Quanlan Tu (Complete Atlas of the Empire), China’s first large-scale national map drawn with modern surveying methods.
It showed that to draw a large country accurately, you have to go out and measure it, not merely copy older maps.

paras.lead: Navigation needed a different kind of “flat”
parts: In 1569, Mercator introduced the conformal cylindrical projection. On that map, a course held at a constant compass bearing can be drawn as a straight line, which is extremely useful for sailing; the cost is that high latitudes are drawn too large. Maps began to serve transoceanic navigation on a large scale, and they also left many people with a lasting false picture of the world’s “shape.”

In the eighteenth century, France’s Cassini family directed a national triangulation and drew more accurate topographic maps. Britain began a systematic triangulation in 1791 and, around 1801, formed the Ordnance Survey, turning national mapping into an ongoing state task.

paras.lead: From paper maps to digital base maps
parts: In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, aerial photography sped up mapping over large areas. After satellite positioning and remote sensing arrived, a location could be “calculated” rather than only “measured.” Electronic maps can be zoomed, searched, and updated with live traffic, while paper maps have receded into professional, educational, and collectors’ use.

The underlying problems have not gone away: coordinate systems have to be unified, data have to be updated, and errors have to be stated clearly. Under a smooth-looking phone map there is still a survey control network, imagery, and countless checks.

Everyone uses maps; few people ask where they come from. Navigation apps have turned maps into everyday infrastructure. National mapping agencies still provide the basic geographic information, and commercial firms add roads, businesses, and live traffic on top. Once accuracy improved, new disputes appeared: how to draw borders, who owns location data, and how to protect privacy.
The more convenient a map becomes, the easier it is to forget that it is also a form of power and a public good.

The Huangyu Quanlan Tu is completed
France and Britain push national surveys
Electronic navigation becomes the most common form of map

blocks.title: A few years in the history of maps

critical.label: Another angle
items: Surveyors and cartographers｜View: Measure the position accurately first, then choose a projection that fits the use.；Stakes: Professional standards and continuity of data.；Worry: The work is misused on an outdated base map or the wrong projection.；Basis: Gains in accuracy from triangulation to satellite positioning.

The state and the military｜View: Maps are infrastructure for government and security.；Stakes: Borders, resources, and mobilization.；Worry: A precise map falls into an opponent’s hands.；Basis: Countries have long treated detailed topographic maps as controlled material.

Sailors, pilots, and drivers｜View: A map has to be usable, not only mathematically elegant.；Stakes: Arriving safely.；Worry: A projection or an update error leads to a wrong judgment.；Basis: Mercator maps are convenient for compass sailing; electronic navigation wins with live traffic.

Commercial map platforms｜View: Turn the base map into a service that can be searched and monetized.；Stakes: Users, advertising, and data.；Worry: Dependence on underlying data, policy limits, and privacy disputes.；Basis: Navigation apps have become the most common way into a map.

Ordinary residents｜View: They want both not to get lost and not to be tracked too closely by location data.；Stakes: Convenience and privacy.；Worry: Their homes and movements become data that can be sold.；Basis: After location services spread, privacy became a new public issue.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: The more precise a map is, the more useful it is—and the more sensitive.
A projection that helps navigation can give people a wrong impression of how large countries are.
Commercial firms make maps easier to use, but the basic surveying still depends heavily on public investment.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Technology can already place a person within a few meters, or even less. The next hard questions are: who updates the map, to whom it is opened, and by what rules contested lines are drawn.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Judgments of how accurate ancient maps were depend on whether one uses modern standards or the maps’ original uses; the conclusions will differ.
How different versions of the Huangyu Quanlan Tu circulated and were copied is a matter for specialized map history.
The real-time accuracy of electronic maps varies widely by place and signal conditions, and cannot be summed up in a single number.

pieces.title: Barely a month after fundraising, they must show their holdings every day: the first active ETFs list
pieces.hook: Publishing holdings every day reduces information asymmetry; it does not automatically mean better returns. In the early days after listing, it is more useful to watch bid-ask…
pieces.takeaway: Publishing holdings every day reduces information asymmetry; it does not automatically mean better returns. In the early days after listing, what is more worth watching is the bid-ask spread, premiums or discounts, and trading volume, and whether the actual industry mix and style match the product’s positioning—that is the framework offered by Xu Yanhong, chief analyst on the fund-evaluation team at China Merchants Securities. The facts already checked are that the products have listed, the rules are in writing, and fundraising size and portfolio-building progress can be found in announcements. The inference that should be kept separate is this: transparency will change who has an information edge, but weekly net-value moves during the closed period are not enough to grade a manager’s skill.
pieces.event: Listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges on 2026-11-23; fundraising began on 10-23; registered on 10-19

parts: On November 23, China’s first 18 actively managed exchange-traded funds (active ETFs) were formally listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges. Fundraising began on October 23, exactly a month before listing; the products were registered on October 19.

All 18 funds hit the 2 billion yuan fundraising cap and closed the offer early; 17 of them, being oversubscribed, used pro-rata allocation. Together they raised 36 billion yuan. An active ETF lets the manager pick stocks, time the market, and set the mix, rather than tracking a given index; at the same time, the shares can be bought and sold during the trading day like an ordinary ETF, and created or redeemed in kind.

How they differ from ordinary funds and ordinary ETFs: traditional equity funds usually disclose holdings quarterly, and often only the top ten positions, so the data lag. Under the exchanges’ rules for actively managed ETFs, the manager must, before the market opens on each trading day, publish a creation and redemption basket through designated channels, based on the actual portfolio.

Holdings thus move from a quarterly update to a daily one, and the disclosure is the full book, not only the top ten. Unlike a passive ETF that tracks an index, an active ETF’s aim is not to copy an index but to try to beat a benchmark. Xue Hongyan, a deputy director at Star Map Financial Research Institute, said the biggest difference between the two lies in the investment objective.

The first batch covers five strategies—balanced, value, dividend, quality, and growth—and includes both fundamental stock-picking and quantitative approaches. The management fee is 1% in every case, below the average for actively managed equity funds.

paras.lead: The rules write transparency and constraints together
parts: The rules do not only require “publication.” A fund must hold no fewer than 30 securities, and the top ten positions together may not exceed 60% of net asset value. Stocks it holds must have had, over the past year, an average daily turnover in the top 80% of all listed shares on their exchange.

The exchanges also require turnover to be kept in a reasonable range, to avoid frequent short-term trading and large, concentrated portfolio shifts. There is a timetable for building positions as well. On November 2, a responsible official at a relevant department of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) said the regulator would guide and encourage the 18 active ETFs that had finished fundraising to build their positions faster.

According to listing announcements cited by Securities Daily, as of November 16 the 18 products had an average equity position of 56.71%, and the pace was uneven. Under the rules, the equity share must reach the 80% line set in the fund contract before listing. Holdings were mainly in manufacturing, finance, and mining; among the top ten positions, banks, electronics, and food and beverage had the larger shares, and the style was mostly balanced and value-oriented.

During the closed period, net asset value is disclosed only on Fridays. Unit values among the 18 products have already diverged: some are above the 1 yuan par value, and some are below it. Lin Xinlong, manager of the Tianhong Balanced Quantitative Active ETF, cautioned that the observable sample is still small, and it should not be used to judge a manager’s ability to earn excess returns.

paras.lead: Who benefits, and who is under pressure
parts: For investors preparing to trade these shares, they can deal during the session, the fees are lower, holdings are visible every day, and it is easier both to adjust and to monitor. For fund managers, transparency is a selling point and also a constraint: once the portfolio is changed, the market can see it quickly, and there is a risk of being copied or traded ahead of.

Lin Xinlong said they would bring liquidity, strategy capacity, and trading costs into their decisions, and would face that risk squarely. For index ETFs and traditional active funds, this is a new kind of competition: they face a more transparent, tradable active product, and they still have to show that their fees and disclosure frequency are justified.

For regulators, the 36 billion yuan in total is seen as additional money that can enter the market; but the rules also require portfolios to stay relatively stable, so the new tool does not become a channel for short-term speculation.

blocks.title: Positions and fees of the first active ETFs

critical.label: Another angle
items: Investors who subscribed and plan to trade｜View: If they pay a management fee, they should see the portfolio more promptly, and they can also make their own decisions during the session.；Stakes: Lower fees, greater transparency, and more trading flexibility.；Worry: Spreads and premiums or discounts are wide just after listing, or short-term net value is treated as proof of skill.；Basis: Intraday trading; daily creation and redemption baskets; Xu Yanhong’s advice to watch spreads, premiums or discounts, and volume first.

Fund managers and portfolio managers｜View: The value of active management lies in stock-picking and allocation, not in copying an index.；Stakes: Grow assets, show research skill, and keep charging fees under more transparent rules.；Worry: Holdings are copied or traded ahead of, and strategy capacity is constrained.；Basis: Lin Xinlong has spoken publicly about the tracking risk created by transparency; Yang Jinghan stresses allocating by intrinsic value and not paying a premium for short-term heat.

Traditional active funds and passive index ETFs｜View: The new tool puts “active” together with “tradable and see-through,” so existing products have to show they are still worth their fees or their way of tracking.；Stakes: Keep assets and clients.；Worry: Money flows to new products that disclose more often and trade more easily.；Basis: Traditional funds usually report the top ten holdings quarterly; passive ETFs track an index and generally do not pick stocks actively.

The CSRC and the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges｜View: Additional money can be brought in, but transparency and stability must be written into the rules.；Stakes: Liven the market, complete the product range, and curb short-term speculation.；Worry: The new tool is used for frequent trading, or positions are built too slowly and trading is disorderly after listing.；Basis: On November 2 the CSRC encouraged faster position-building; the guidelines require daily disclosure of the actual portfolio and control of turnover and concentration.

Securities firms and liquidity providers｜View: A new on-exchange product will create demand for trading and market-making.；Stakes: Volume and spread income.；Worry: Liquidity is thin at first, or investors do not understand premiums and discounts.；Basis: Active ETFs can trade during the session and be created or redeemed in kind; their premiums, discounts, and bid-ask spreads are key things to watch just after listing.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: The more transparent it is, the easier it is for investors to monitor—and the easier it is for others to copy or trade ahead.

The 36 billion yuan is additional money regulators want to see, but a week before listing the average position was still below the contractual 80% line; there is a trade-off between the speed of building positions and the impact on the market.
A 1% management fee is lower than that of many active equity funds, yet managers still have to show, under daily disclosure, that they can earn excess returns.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The dispute is not about “whether to be transparent,” but about how much of an advantage active management can keep, once the full book is published every day, that cannot be copied at once—and whether investors will judge by the year, or by the first few days of net value.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: A figure for the number of effective subscribers often appears in reprints; the first-hand source is not solid enough, and this article does not use a specific count.

Whether every product had reached an 80% equity position between November 16 and the listing date must be checked against the latest announcements. This article confirms only the average at that time and the requirement in the rules.
“Below the average fee for active equity funds” is a comparison in the reporting; this article has not independently calculated a market-wide average fee.
The direction of position-building comes from a summary of the listing announcements, not from holdings after listing.

pieces.title: 330 votes locked in the 258th seat: the House has its largest majority in thirty years
pieces.short: The largest House majority in thirty years
pieces.hook: To treat a flip decided by 330 votes as a symbol of a national wave—or, conversely, as “only a fluke”—lacks…
pieces.takeaway: To treat a flip decided by 330 votes as a symbol of a national wave—or, conversely, as “only a fluke”—lacks enough evidence. The more careful course is to record it as a verified change in scale, and to leave whether the promises are kept to the next 100 days.
pieces.event: 2026-11-22: the seat count was locked after the recount in North Carolina’s 5th District
pieces.imageAlt: Official congressional portrait of Hakeem Jeffries
pieces.imageCredit: United States Congress · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On November 22 (Sunday), a recount was completed in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District. Democrat Chuck Hubbard, leading by 330 votes, defeated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx, chair of the House Rules Committee.

In a statement, Foxx said she had called Hubbard to concede. Figures from the North Carolina State Board of Elections showed Hubbard ahead by 330 votes after the recount. The result pushed Democrats to at least 258 seats in the House.

CBS, citing the Associated Press, said this was the largest majority either party had won in a House election in thirty years, and the largest since 1992. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called it the largest majority in Congress this century. Democrats have so far gained a net 44 seats, four more than the 40 seats they gained in the 2018 midterms during Trump’s first term.

Republicans will hold at least 173 seats. In a 435-seat House, four races remain unresolved: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will go to December runoffs. So 258 is a confirmed floor, not a final total.

The timing needs to be stated clearly: after the midterm elections in early November, Democrats had already secured a House majority. What November 22 changed was not a first crossing of the halfway line, but the locking-in of a majority on a scale rarely seen in thirty years. NBC’s figures also noted that Trump had carried Foxx’s district by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024.

paras.lead: What a larger majority can do
parts: In the House, passing a bill usually takes 218 votes. CBS noted that if Jeffries is elected speaker on January 3, 2027, he could still allow dozens of his own members to vote no, even if every Republican opposed the bill.

That stands in contrast to the past two years, when Republican Speaker Mike Johnson had to keep the chamber running on a single-digit majority. Democrats also hold the Senate. CBS said Senate Democrats will have 56 of 100 seats, the largest edge in more than a decade; later reports, including in USA Today, also use a 56–44 count, which includes two independents who caucus with the Democrats.

The White House remains in the hands of Republican President Trump, creating divided government. Jeffries’s side has set out a 100-day agenda: rapid votes to reverse Medicaid cuts advanced by Republicans, and to restore Affordable Care Act tax credits that Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats also plan to use subpoena power to open a series of investigations. Jeffries has not ruled out a third impeachment of Trump. Representative Tom Suozzi, a New York Democrat and a former accountant, argues that about 75% of the time should go to living costs and 25% to accountability.

What voters wanted: the household bill, or a larger majority? CBS exit polls showed that voters who thought the economy was poor voted Democratic in the House elections. For the second time in a row, a majority of respondents called inflation a burden on daily life; more people said their finances were worse than two years earlier, and those voters also leaned Democratic.

The reporting also listed high prices, the war with Iran, and concerns about corruption as the background to voters’ dissatisfaction. On the November 22 edition of CBS’s Face the Nation, Jeffries said: “If over the next two years we get nothing done on affordability, health care, and immigration, can you imagine how angry the American people will be at Washington?

” The White House has warned against the proposed investigations, even saying such inquiries could constitute “blatant criminal conduct.” Representative Jim Jordan, a Republican, has become minority leader and said the next two years would be spent “fighting for American families.”

paras.lead: A narrative frame to watch carefully
parts: One story is a “historic mandate”: more seats mean a larger agenda must be pushed through. Another is a “punishment of the governing party”: voters wanted a change in prices and in the war, not necessarily a blank check for the new majority. 258 seats are already large, but legislation still has to get past Senate rules, a presidential veto, and divisions inside the Democratic Party.

Four unresolved races mean the total can still change. To treat a flip decided by 330 votes as a symbol of a national wave—or, conversely, as “only a fluke”—lacks enough evidence. The more careful course is to record it as a verified change in scale, and to leave whether the promises are kept to the next 100 days.

The recount in North Carolina’s 5th ends; Foxx concedes; Democrats reach at least 258 seats
Four races remain unresolved, including two Louisiana runoffs in December
The new House elects a speaker and takes over the agenda

critical.label: Another angle
items: House Democrats and Jeffries｜View: This is the largest House majority of the century, and they should move quickly on living costs, health care, and oversight.；Stakes: Turn 258 seats into bills that can pass, and take the speakership in January 2027.；Worry: If they get nothing done in two years on affordability, health care, and immigration, voters will turn their anger on the new majority.；Basis: Jeffries’s “largest majority of the century” remark, and his warning on Face the Nation about public anger; public descriptions of the 100-day agenda and the investigation plans.

House Republicans, and the former-majority wing Foxx represented｜View: Even with far fewer seats, they should still block the other side’s agenda from the minority, and try to win the chamber back in two years.；Stakes: Keep a voice with at least 173 seats, and mobilize the party around investigations and impeachment.；Worry: Losing a district Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024 will be written as a broader warning.；Basis: Foxx conceded after the recount; Jordan became minority leader and said he would “fight for American families”; NBC’s figures on the 2024 presidential margin in that district.

The White House and Trump｜View: Congressional investigations are an attack on executive power; the new majority cannot turn oversight into an unbounded settling of scores.；Stakes: Keep the veto, and limit subpoenas and inquiries into the White House and family wealth.；Worry: A comfortable House majority makes investigations harder to stall by procedure.；Basis: The White House warning that proposed investigations could constitute “blatant criminal conduct”; under divided government the president can still veto legislation.

Voters who shifted to Democrats over prices, the war, or concerns about corruption｜View: The vote was a protest against high prices and the current government’s record, and does not automatically mean support for any one bill.；Stakes: Living costs, medical costs, and results they can feel.；Worry: The new majority treats a “historic victory” as a mandate that can be cashed in slowly.；Basis: In CBS exit polls, voters who thought the economy was poor, or whose finances were worse than two years earlier, leaned Democratic; the reporting listed inflation, the Iran war, and concerns about corruption.

Candidates and voters in the four unresolved districts｜View: The national story has already been written as a “historic majority,” but local ballots may still change the final count.；Stakes: The December runoffs and results that are still being counted.；Worry: Being treated as a footnote, with local issues ignored.；Basis: One race each remains in Minnesota and Tennessee, and two Louisiana seats go to December runoffs; 258 and 173 are both confirmed floors.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: A more comfortable majority reduces the damage of no votes inside the party, but it raises the political cost of having to deliver results.
The White House keeps the veto; the House expands its investigative power; oversight and confrontation will heat up at the same time.
Suozzi’s split of about 75% for living costs and 25% for accountability shows that Democrats do not have only one formula for “legislate first or investigate first.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The dispute is not whether 258 is a thirty-year record, but whether it should be read as a mandate, a punishment, or a temporary ceiling that still faces a veto and unresolved districts.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Exit polls show voting leanings; they cannot precisely measure how many seats were decided by the “Iran war” or by “corruption,” each on its own.
Whether Jeffries is elected speaker on January 3 still depends on votes from his own members; it is not a settled fact.
Four unresolved races may change the final count; 258 to 173 is not a final score.
“The largest majority this century” and “the largest since 1992” both rest on 258, but historical comparisons by different organizations differ slightly; the seat count itself should be the standard.
